title: Chapter 128 — The Pequod Meets The Rachel
paragraphs: Next day, a large ship, the Rachel, was sighted bearing straight down on the Pequod, all her spars thickly clustered with men. At the time the Pequod was making good speed through the water; but as the broad-winged stranger shot close to her from windward, her boastful sails all fell slack together like empty bladders that have burst, and all life fled from the stricken hull.
"Bad news; she brings bad news," muttered the old Manxman. But before her commander, who stood up in his boat with his trumpet to his mouth — before he could hail hopefully, Ahab's voice was heard.
"Aye, yesterday. Have you seen a whale-boat adrift?"

Throttling his joy, Ahab answered no to this unexpected question, and would then gladly have boarded the stranger, when the stranger's captain himself, having stopped his vessel, was seen climbing down her side. A few sharp pulls at the oars, and his boat-hook soon gripped the Pequod's main-chains, and he sprang onto the deck. Ahab immediately recognized him as a Nantucketer he knew. But no formal greeting was exchanged.
"Where was he? — not killed! — not killed!" cried Ahab, pressing close to him. "How did it happen?"

It seemed that rather late on the previous afternoon, three of the stranger's boats had been engaged with a shoal of whales that had led them some four or five miles from the ship; and while they were still in swift chase to windward, the white hump and head of Moby Dick had suddenly loomed up out of the water, not very far to leeward. At that, the fourth rigged boat — a reserve one — had been instantly lowered to give chase. After a keen sail before the wind, this fourth boat — the swiftest-keeled of all — seemed to have succeeded in fastening to him; at least, as far as the man at the mast-head could tell anything about it. In the distance he saw the boat shrunk to a dot; then a swift gleam of bubbling white water; and after that, nothing more. From this it was concluded that the stricken whale must have run away with his pursuers for some indefinite distance, as often happens. There was some apprehension, but as yet no real alarm. The recall signals were hoisted in the rigging; darkness came on; and since the ship had to pick up her three boats far to windward before going in search of the fourth in exactly the opposite direction, she had not only been forced to leave that boat to its fate until nearly midnight, but for the time being to increase her distance from it. But once the rest of her crew were at last safe aboard, she crowded on all sail — studding-sail on studding-sail — after the missing boat, lighting a fire in her try-pots as a beacon, with every other man aloft on the lookout. But though she then sailed far enough to reach the presumed spot where the missing men were last seen; though she then stopped to lower her spare boats to row all around her; and, finding nothing, had dashed on again, stopped again, and lowered her boats again; and though she had kept doing this until daylight — still not the least glimpse of the missing keel had been seen.

Having told the story, the stranger captain at once went on to reveal why he had boarded the Pequod. He wanted her to join his own ship in the search, the two of them sailing over the sea some four or five miles apart, on parallel lines, and so sweeping a double horizon, as it were.

"I will wager something now," whispered Stubb to Flask, "that someone in that missing boat went off wearing that captain's best coat; maybe his watch — he's so cursed anxious to get it back. Who ever heard of two pious whale-ships cruising after one missing whale-boat in the height of the whaling season? See, Flask, only see how pale he looks — pale in the very buttons of his eyes — look — it wasn't the coat — it must have been the —"

"My boy, my own boy is among them. For God's sake — I beg you, I implore you" — so the stranger captain now cried out to Ahab, who until then had received his plea with nothing but ice. "Let me charter your ship for forty-eight hours — I will gladly pay for it, and pay handsomely — if there is no other way — for forty-eight hours only — only that — you must, oh, you must, and you shall do this thing."
"His son!" cried Stubb, "oh, it's his son he's lost! I take back the coat and watch — what does Ahab say? We must save that boy."
"He's drowned with the rest of them, last night," said the old Manx sailor standing behind them. "I heard; all of you heard their spirits."

Now, as it soon turned out, what made this incident of the Rachel's all the more melancholy was that not only was one of the captain's sons among the missing boat's crew, but among the crews of the other boats — which had at the same time been separated from the ship in the other direction during the dark confusion of the chase — there had been yet another son. So for a time the wretched father was plunged to the very bottom of the cruelest perplexity, which was only resolved for him when his chief mate instinctively adopted a whale-ship's ordinary procedure in such emergencies: when caught between endangered but divided boats, always pick up the majority first. But the captain, for some unknown reason of temperament, had refrained from mentioning all this, and not until Ahab's iciness forced him to it did he speak of his one still-missing boy — a little lad, only twelve years old, whose father, with the earnest but untroubled boldness of a Nantucketer's paternal love, had sought this early to initiate him into the perils and wonders of a calling that had been, almost from time immemorial, the destiny of all his race. Nor is it uncommon for Nantucket captains to send a son of such tender age away from them, on a long three or four years' voyage in some ship other than their own, so that the boy's first knowledge of a whaleman's career will not be weakened by any chance display of a father's natural but ill-timed favoritism, or undue anxiety and concern.
Meanwhile the stranger was still begging his poor favor of Ahab; and Ahab still stood like an anvil, taking every blow without the least quiver of his own.

"I will not go," said the stranger, "until you say yes to me. Do to me as you would have me do to you in the same case. For you, too, have a boy, Captain Ahab — though only a child, and nestling safely at home now — a child of your old age, too. Yes, yes, you relent; I see it — run, run, men, now, and stand by to square in the yards."

"Avast," cried Ahab — "don't touch a rope-yarn"; then, in a voice that drew out and shaped every word — "Captain Gardiner, I will not do it. Even now I am losing time. Good-bye, good-bye. God bless you, man, and may I forgive myself, but I must go. Mr. Starbuck, look at the binnacle watch, and three minutes from this very instant warn off all strangers; then brace forward again, and let the ship sail as before."

Turning hurriedly, with his face averted, he went down into his cabin, leaving the stranger captain transfixed at this unconditional and utter rejection of so earnest a plea. But starting out of his trance, Gardiner silently hurried to the side, more fell than stepped into his boat, and returned to his ship.

Soon the two ships' wakes parted; and as long as the strange vessel stayed in view, she was seen to yaw this way and that toward every dark spot on the sea, however small. This way and that her yards were swung round; to starboard and to larboard she kept tacking; now she beat against a head sea, and now it pushed her before it; while all the while her masts and yards were thickly clustered with men, like three tall cherry trees when the boys are up among the boughs picking cherries.

But from her still faltering course and her winding, sorrowful path, you could plainly see that this ship, weeping spray as she went, still had not been comforted. She was Rachel, weeping for her children, because they were not.
